blocks.html: FIFE

• Feelings – How does your disease/symptom make you feel?
  • Ideas – What do you think is wrong?
  • Function – How are your symptoms impacting your function/enjoyment of life?
  • Expectations – What do you hope to get out of the medical visit?
Choosing Wisely Canada

• 1. Consider the least invasive testing option first
  • 2. Only order tests which will change patient management
  • 3. Discuss and educate patients on whether tests are necessary
  • 4. Seek clarification if you believe something was ordered unnecessarily
  • 5. Do NOT recommend tests exclusively for the learning experience
  • 6. Do NOT recommend tests in anticipation of preceptor preference
ADL and IADL

• Activities of daily living (ADL): feeding, dressing, bathing, walking – deficits may indicate home healthcare/nursing facility
  • Instrumental activities of daily living (IADL): cooking, cleaning, transportation, laundry, managing finances – improve QOL
The 4 Ps

• Predisposing factors: put an individual at risk of developing a problem
  • Precipitating factors: a specific event/trigger to the onset of the current problem
  • Perpetuating factors: maintain the problem once it has become established
  • Protective factors: strengths of the individual that reduce the severity of the problem
WHO-6-Steps of Rational Prescribing

• 1. Patient’s problem – symptoms, diagnosis, patient characteristics
  • 2. Therapeutic objective – curative, symptomatic, preventative
  • 3. Treatment choice – contraindications, interactions, comedications
  • 4. Start treatment – write Rx
  • 5. Give patient information – instructions, warnings

blocks.html: Levels of Prevention

• Health promotion/primordial prevention – entire population; prevent risk factors, lower average population risk
  • Primary prevention – 1+ risk factors; manage risk factors, prevent development of disease
  • Secondary prevention – limited disease; early diagnosis, prompt Tx, prevent disease progression/recurrence
  • Tertiary prevention – symptomatic/advanced disease; reduce complications/disability
Approaches to Disease Prevention and Control

• Clinical/individual-centered approach – causes of cases
  • Public health/population-based approach – causes of disease incidence
  • High-risk strategy – seeks to identify high-risk susceptible individuals
  • Population strategy – seeks to control the determinants of incidence and lower mean level/shift the distribution of risk factors
  • Prevention paradox: prevention that brings large benefits to the community offers little to each participating individual
The Chronic Disease Continuum
Risk: probability that a specific action/exposure will give rise to a negative health outcome
Risk factor: individual characteristics or behaviours that increase the likelihood that a
person will suffer negative health outcomes

• Smoking, alcohol, diet, physical activity Risk condition: chronic condition that contributes to risk of disease/disability/death

blocks.html: Ethical Theories

• Deontology/Kantianism – based on pure reason and duty; never treat others merely as a means to an end
  • Utilitarianism – maximize utility and minimize bad
  • Principlism/pluralistic theory – autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice
  • Casuistry – bottom-up reasoning; inferring from similar past cases
  • Narrative ethics – reflection and drawing broader lessons; personal identity and storytelling; highly contextual/subjective
  • Feminist/communitarian ethics – critical of mainstream bioethics that neglect women’s issues/perspectives
  • Pragmatism – looks for a 3rd “outside the box” solution
  • Virtue ethics – focused on character of the individual; pursue eudaemonia; balance character traits between vices
Practical Ethical Decision-Making

• 1. Recognition – gather and manage appropriate data considering the relevant values
  • 2. Designation – clarify the goals and describe the ethical conflict
  • 3. Evaluation – explain why this problem exists, distinguish the cause, and highlight ethical issues
  • 4. Clarification – evaluate the feasible options and identify the implications
  • 5. Determination – decide the “best” solution to the problem
  • 6. Implementation – take action to implement with an established evaluation process

blocks.html: Cultural Competence

• Cultural destructiveness: forced assimilation, subjugation, rights and privileges for dominant groups only
  • Cultural incapacity: racism, maintain stereotypes, unfair hiring practices
  • Cultural blindness: differences ignored, treat everyone the same, only meet needs of dominant groups
  • Cultural pre-competence: expose cultural issues, are committed, assess needs of organization/individuals
  • Cultural competence: recognize individual/cultural differences, seek advice from diverse groups, interact effectively
  • Cultural proficiency: implement changes to improve services based upon cultural needs
  • Cultural safety: fostering an environment that is spiritually, socially, and emotionally safe
  • Cultural humility: recognition that our own perspective is not the only and not necessarily the “correct” perspective
10 Things to Know About the Health of Refugees and Migrants (WHO)

• 1. The health of refugees/migrants is important – basic human right
  • 2. The numbers of migrants are often overestimated
  • 3. Refugees/migrants are likely to be healthy in general
  • 4. Refugees/migrants can face challenges in accessing health care – legal status, language barriers, discrimination
  • 5. Refugees/migrants have a lower risk for all forms of cancer, except cervical cancer, but more diabetes than the host population
  • 6. Breakdown in health systems in the country of origin
  • 7. PTSD seems to be more prevalent among refugees and asylum seekers than the host population
  • 8. Labour migrants constitute the largest group of migrants globally – more work-related injuries
  • 9. Children without parents or a guardian are especially vulnerable
  • 10. Making health systems refugee- and migrant-friendly

• Red fibers – slow-twitch, high myoglobin, high mitochondria

The Sarcomere and the Sliding Filament Model

• I band = isotropic; divided by a Z line (disc)
  • A band = anisotropic; divided by an H zone and M line
  • Sarcomere = Z line to Z line; functional unit of muscle
  • I bands and H zones shorten during muscle contraction, sarcomeres shorten
  • Troponin complex = T-troponin (tropomyosin binding activity), I-troponin (inhibitory activity – binds actin), C-troponin (calcium binding activity)
  • Tropomyosin = binds actin and blocks myosin binding in the absence of Ca2+
Neurons

• Motor neurons (efferent) – multipolar neurons convey impulses from brain, spinal cord, and ganglia to effector cells
  • Sensory neurons (afferent) – pseudo-unipolar or bipolar neurons in ganglia convey impulses from receptors to the CNS
  • Integrative (interneurons) – multipolar neurons form integrating networks between sensory and motor neurons
  • Axonal transport on microtubules needed to deliver vesicles to synapse
  • Neurons do NOT divide, but can have peripheral nerve repair; sprouts generated, Schwann cells re-innervate the muscle
Myelination

• Schwann cells (PNS) – one cell myelinates only a segment of a single axon
  • Oligodendrocytes (CNS) – one cell myelinates many axons
  • Myelin sheath consists of concentric layers of lipid membranes and proteins that insulate the axon
Nervous System Supporting Cells

• Astrocytes – form a scaffolded network in the CNS between capillaries, fibers, and neurons; maintain blood-brain barrier
  • Microglia – transform into phagocytic cells in damaged CNS; defence system; migratory
  • Ependymal cells – form the simple epithelial lining of the ventricles and spinal canal; ciliated for propulsion of CSF
Homeostatic Control Systems

• Sensors – detect changes and transmit an input signal
  • Integrating centers – process the information
  • Effectors – receive and process the output signal

TBW = total body water (60% of body weight)
ICF = intercellular fluid (K+)
ECF = extracellular fluid (Na+, Cl-)

blocks.html: Cellular Transport

• Simple diffusion – passive transport, concentration gradient; small lipophilic molecules (O2, CO2, steroid hormones, alcohol)
  • Facilitated diffusion – carrier proteins, concentration gradient; larger polar molecules
  • Active transport – carrier-mediated transport, against concentration gradient, requires ATP; Na+/K+ pump, Ca2+ pump
  • Primary – energy is derived directly from the breakdown of ATP
  • Secondary – uses the potential energy from the concentration gradient generated by a primary transport Symport = same direction; antiport = opposite directions
  • Osmosis – movement of water down its concentration gradient Osmolality = # of Osmol/kg of water
  • Osmolarity = # of Osmol/L of solution; ECF osmolarity = 290mOsM
  • Tonicity: the ability of a solution to cause osmosis across a biological membrane
  • Factors that affect the rate of diffusion through cell membranes: concentration gradient, lipid solubility, molecular size, membrane area, composition of lipid layer
Cell Signalling

• Autocrine signalling – cell signals to itself
  • Paracrine signalling – release of chemical messengers over relatively short distances
  • Cell-cell contact signalling – intracellular mediators diffuse between gap junctions
  • Synaptic signalling – nerve cells transmit signals via release of neurotransmitters
  • Endocrine signalling – hormones are produced by specialized cells and released into the bloodstream, and travel to target cells
Resting Membrane Potential

• RMP = -70 mV
  • Highly permeable to K+ and slightly permeable to Na+ and Cl-
  • K+ and Cl- are the most important ions involved in the generation of the RMP
  • Leak potassium channels contribute to the establishment of a negative RMP
  • Na+/K+ pump maintains the concentration gradient for Na+ and K+ by moving 3 Na+ OUT and 2 K+ IN
The Action Potential

• All-or-none response and unidirectional
  • Depolarization: movement of the membrane potential towards zero
  • Threshold: voltage at which an action potential is triggered
  • Repolarization: return of the membrane potential to its resting value
  • Hyperpolarization: movement of the membrane potential to more negative values
  • Absolute refractory period: no stimulus will excite the nerve; inactivated V.G. Na+ channels
  • Relative refractory period: stronger than normal stimulus is required; some V.G. Na+ channels have recovered
  • 1. Stimulate nerve
  • 2. Membrane depolarizes (-70 mV to -55 mV)
  • 3. V.G. Na+ channels open very rapidly
  • 4. Na+ flows into the cell
  • 5. Action potential is initiated
  • 6. Membrane depolarizes rapidly to +45 mV
  • 7. V.G. K+ channels begin opening while V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated
  • 8. Eventually all V.G. K+ channels are open and all V.G. Na+ channels are inactivated
  • 9. K+ rushes out of the cell
  • 10. Membrane repolarizes (+45 mV to -70 mV)
  • 11. K+ continues to leave the cell as V.G. K+ channels close slowly
  • 12. Membrane hyperpolarizes to -90 mV
  • 13. V.G. K+ channels close
  • 14. Membrane potential returns to normal (-70 mV) and V.G. channels return to resting configuration
Neuromuscular Junction

• Motor neuro pre-synaptic axon terminal – filled with synaptic vesicles
  • Synaptic cleft – space between the pre- and post-synaptic cells
  • Post-synaptic membrane of skeletal muscle fiber
  • 1. AP on motor nerve depolarizes axon terminal and V.G. Ca2+ channels open
  • 2. Ca2+ flows in and Ach is released – larger [Ca2+] = more Ach
  • 3. Ach diffuses across the synaptic cleft to the end plate
  • 4. Ach binds to nicotinic receptors and chemically gated channels open
  • 5. Na+ flows into the muscle cell and K+ flows out – local depolarization, so no AP yet
  • 6. Depolarization causes an end plate potential (EPP)
  • 7. EPP triggers V.G Na+ channels to open, triggering an AP
Excitation contraction coupling (ECC)

• 8. AP generated at the end plate of the muscle cell propagates over the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules
  • 9. Voltage sensors in the T-tubule detect the AP and change shape
  • 10. Voltage sensor opens Ca2+ channels on the lateral sac of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
  • 11. Ca2+ binds to troponin, causing tropomyosin to roll off the myosin binding sites found on actin
  • 12. Myosin attaches to actin (crossbridge formation) and power stroke occurs
  • 13. Actin (thin myofilaments) slides over myosin (thick myofilaments) and muscle contracts (sliding filaments)
  • The muscle will continue contracting as long as there are stimuli at the NMJ, Ach is available, and Ca2+ are in the sarcoplasm
  • Relaxation – Ach is broken down by acetylcholinesterase and taken back up into the axon terminal; Ca2+ is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by Ca2+ ATPase; tropomyosin covers myosin binding sites and muscle relaxes
  • Thin myofilaments – G-Actin (myosin binding sites), tropomyosin (covers myosin binding sites), troponin (regulatory protein)
  • Thick myofilaments – many individual myosin molecules (heads contain actin binding sites and ATP binding sites)
Electrodiagnostic Testing

• Myopathy: nerve conduction can be normal, but compound muscle amplitude is reduced
  • Neuropathy: nerve conduction is expected to be abnormal, especially in demyelination diseases
  • Nerve conduction studies – evaluates the speed and strength of conduction of an AP by the nerve fiber
  • Electromyography – measures the direct electrical activity of the muscle; evaluates insertional and resting activity of muscles
  • Repetitive nerve stimulation – nerve fiber is stimulated in a repetitive fashion and the response is recorded from the muscles

Bone Cells

blocks.html: Imaging

• Radiograph – radiation x-rays; need a minimum of 2 radiographs at 90° (anteroposterior, posteroanterior, lateral, oblique)
  • Silhouetting: anatomical structures become distinguishable on radiographs due to different tissue opacities that surround the structure Summation/superimposition: overlapping of structures; may mislead the reader into thinking there is an abnormality
  • Cannot differentiate muscles and tendons; cannot visualize the brain and internal joint structures
  • CT – radiation x-rays; thin 3D slices (axial)
  • Voxel: small 2D measurement of volume Accuracy and precision increases the likelihood that small lesions and abnormalities will be detected
  • Can visualize the brain and heart; cannot visualize internal joint structures
  • More expensive, much larger dose of ionizing radiation
  • Not recommended for pregnant women
  • MRI – powerful magnet and radio waves
  • Echo time (TE): measurement of the energy signal received at a specific time after the radiofrequency coil pulse Repetition time (TR): measurement of the signals received as the pulse is turned on and off
  • T1-weighted image: TE and TR are short – show fat best, but are fat-suppressed; mostly grey/black image
  • T2-weighted: TE and TR are long – show damaged or pathologic tissue (fluids) best; bright signal
  • Proton density weighted image: TE is short and TR is long – reveal dense tissue well (cartilage, tendon and joint pain)
  • Most expensive, longest time to produce an image Contraindications: cardiac pacemakers, cochlear implants, ferro-magnetic metal implants

• Evidence-Based Medicine
  • Evidence-based medicine = clinical judgement + scientific evidence + patient preference and values
• Clinical significance: value =

• Medical reversal: when a new clinical trial, superior to predecessors by virtue of better controls, design, size, or endpoints, contradicts current clinical practice; undermines trust in the medical system
  • Critical appraisal: process of carefully and systematically assessing the outcome of scientific research to judge its trustworthiness, value, and relevance in a particular context PICO framework: patient/problem/population, intervention, comparison/control/comparator, outcomes
  • Meta-analysis: combines individual effects of a number of studies addressing the same question to produce a summary effect
  • Randomized controlled trials: allocation of subjects to experimental or control group by chance
  • Simple randomization, block randomization, stratified randomization
  • Prospective cohort study: exposure and non-exposure are confirmed as they occur during the study
  • Retrospective cohort study: exposure is confirmed from past records
  • Case-control study: cases are compared with controls with respect to exposure Incident cases = newly diagnosed; can identify risk factors, but must wait a period of time and excludes deaths
  • Prevalent cases = diagnosed for a period of time; can study right away, but may identify characteristics of survival

• Cross-sectional study: exposure and outcome are measured at the same point in time
  • Case report/series: detailed description of one or a few cases without a control group
  • Blinding – open label (all parties aware), single blind (patient/clinician unaware), double blind (patient + investigator unaware), triple blind (patient + investigator + analysts unaware), unblinding (disclosure of allocation)
  • Confounder: an extraneous variable whose presence affects the variables being studied so that the results do not reflect the actual relationship between the variables under study
  • Lead time: the interval between the diagnosis made by a screening program (preclinical phase) and the diagnosis made by the presentation of signs and symptoms (clinical phase)
  • Intention-to-treat: analysis of study groups according to the treatment they were assigned, NOT what they received, if any
  • Per-protocol analysis: only includes patients who completed the treatment they were originally allocated
  • Number needed to treat (NNT): an estimate of the number of individuals that would need to be treated with the new therapy
to prevent one negative outcome; NNT = $%!# (/ '/!$#%!#0 1$,'&2$%!# (/ !$#%!#0 1$,'&

• Type I error (α): study sample shows a difference between treatment groups when no difference exists
  • Type II error (β): study sample shows no difference between treatment groups when a difference exists
  • Power: the probability of finding a treatment difference between groups when a true difference exists; power = 1 −𝛽
  • One-sided test: investigators suspect the difference in response rate between the two groups in one direction only
  • Two-sided test: investigators are unsure of the direction of the difference in response rate between the two groups
  • Internal validity – correct study methodology
  • External validity – representativity of the reference population, generalizability
  • Reliability – intrasubject variation, intraobserver variation, interobserver variation
  • Sensitivity: the ability of a test to identify people with disease; positive disease/positive no disease
  • Specificity: the ability of a test to identify people without a disease; negative no disease/no disease
  • Positive predictive value (PPV): positive disease/positive disease + positive no disease
  • Negative predictive value (NPV): negative no disease/negative disease + negative no disease
  • Likelihood ratio (LR): ability of a test to change the pre-test into the post-test probability of a disease being present LR > 10, large change; LR = 1, no change; LR < 1, post-test probability < pre-test; LR < 0.1, large change

blocks.html: Notes

• Goals of “Well Baby” Ax
  • 1. Growth – length, weight, head circumference; correct age until 24 months if < 37 weeks gestation USE WHO GROWTH CHARTS
  • Failure to thrive: weight less than 3% and family norm; weight trajectory crosses 2 major % lines
  • Short stature: height less than 3% and family norm
  • BMI > 85% = overweight, BMI > 95% = obese
  • 2. Parent/caregiver concerns
  • 3. Nutrition – feeding, supplementation, stool pattern/urine output
  • 4. Education and advice – injury prevention, behaviour and family issues, environmental health, other issues
  • 5. Development – inquiry and observation of milestones
  • 6. Physical examination
  • 7. Problems and plans/current and new referrals – medical specialist, dietician, speech, audiology, PT, OT, eyes, dental, social
  • 8. Investigations/screening and immunization
Red Flags of Abnormal Development

• Persistence of primitive reflexes
  • No social smiling or responsive vocalization by 2 months
  • Hands still fisted at 4 months
  • No response to sound
  • Not sitting by 9 months
  • Not pointing to objects of interest or desire by 15 months
  • Not standing by 15 months
  • Not walking by 18 months
  • No single words by 18 months
  • Excessive drooling and still mouthing at 18 months
  • Hand preference at less than 2 years
  • Not putting 2 words together by 2 years
  • Lack of eye contact and engagement with other children at 2 years
  • Not standing briefly on one foot at 3 years
  • Speech not intelligible to familiar adults at 3 years
  • Unable to hop at 4 years
  • Unable to stack 10 blocks and draw a circle at 4 years
  • Cannot pick shorter or longer of two lines at 4 years
  • Loss of previously acquired skills
Brain Development

• Pruning: elimination of unused connections and pathways
  • Sculpting: enhancement of frequently used connections and pathways
  • Critical periods: permanent deficit results if the needed stimuli are not received – visual development
  • Sensitive periods: child is primed to receive sensory input; skill acquisition becomes much more difficult if missed – language

blocks.html: Theories of Development

• Gessell (1928) – wrote detailed descriptions of normal child development
  • Erikson (1950) – psychosocial development

• Pavlov & Thorndike – classical conditioning Reinforcement: relationship between a stimulus and response becomes strengthened through repeated association
  • Extinction: relationship between stimulus and response is weakened
  • Generalization: conditioned response becomes linked to a stimulus similar to the initial stimulus
  • Skinner – operant conditioning Positive reinforcement: addition of a positive event that increases the behaviour
  • Negative reinforcement: ending of a negative event that increases the behaviour
  • Punishment: addition of an event that decreases the behaviour Response cost: loss of positive reinforcement that results in decreased behaviour/extinction
  • Piaget – cognitive development

• Families: comprised of married or common-law couples, including same-sex couples, living in the same dwelling with or without children, and lone parents living with at least one child
  • Role in raising children: physical needs, emotional support, education and socialization
  • No evidence that family structure alone is a significant predictor of child health or developmental outcome
  • One person households, numbers of couples without children, and multigenerational families are INCREASING

blocks.html: Genetics Terminology

• Allelic heterogeneity – different variants in the same gene; different phenotypes
  • Locus heterogeneity – mutations in different genes at different chromosomal loci cause the same phenotype
  • Penetrance – fraction of individuals who carry a gene who manifest a specific phenotype Complete = absolutely shows signs; incomplete = may not show signs
  • Anticipation – symptoms of a disorder become more apparent/severe with each new generation; triple repeat disorders
Patterns of Inheritance

rows:

Males and females affected in equal proportions
All forms of transmission present
Dominant negative: mutant protein is produced and adversely affects the function of the normal
protein produced by the other allele, usually by interacting with it
Haploinsufficiency: a single functioning allele of a gene is not sufficient to produce a normal
phenotype; other allele may have a null allele (abnormal protein is not functional, reduced
mRNA/gene product, allele is completely deleted)
Gain of function mutation: increased activity of the normal gene product
Pleiotropy: a pathogenic variant in one gene can cause multiple effects in different organs
Variable expression and penetrance

People with the condition are usually in one sibship in one generation
Males and females affected in equal proportions
Consanguinity increases the number of individuals affected
Cis: one allele may contain more than one variant – individual NOT affected
Trans: two different mutations on different alleles of the same gene – individual affected

blocks.html: Genetic Disorder Consideration

• Developmental delays, dysmorphic features, or congenital malformations
  • Positive family history of a genetic disorder
  • History of 3+ miscarriages/stillbirths, infertility, neonatal deaths
  • Consanguinity/ethnic background – Ashkenazi Jewish (Tay-Sachs, BRCA1, Canavan disease, familial dysautonomia), French Canadian (Tay-Sachs), Mediterranean (β-thalassemia), Southeast Asian (α-thalassemia), Amish/Mennonite and Arab (various rare disorders), African (sickle cell anemia), Caucasian (cystic fibrosis)
  • Cancers – multiple members, early onset (< 50), multiple primaries in 1 individual, occurrence in less commonly affected sex
  • Early onset heart disease/sudden deaths
Ontario Newborn Screening

• Screens for 30 metabolic disorders – most are autosomal recessive
  • Wilson & Junger criteria: disease (serious, natural Hx understood, asymptomatic stage), screening test (acceptable, economical, reliable), management (treatable, available)
  • 1. Metabolic diseases – body is unable to break down certain substances in foods
  • 2. Endocrine diseases – body produces too much or too little of certain hormones
  • 3. Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) – affects the movement of oxygen in the blood
  • 4. Cystic Fibrosis (CF) – causes problems with breathing and growth
  • 5. Severe Combined Immune Deficiency (SCID) – affects the body's ability to fight infections
  • 6. Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) – causes muscle weakness and wasting
  • 7. Critical Congenital Heart Disease (CCHD) – affects the quantity of oxygen in the blood
  • 8. Congenital hearing loss
Preconception Counselling

• Provision of information and support to a couple planning a pregnancy to promote health and reduce risk
  • Primary prevention – review personal and family Hx, and refer if any genetic conditions present Folic acid: 0.8-1mg/d beginning 3 months prior to pregnancy, continue through 1st trimester
  • Avoid smoking, alcohol, drugs, and exposure to saunas/heat stress
  • Secondary prevention – discuss options for prenatal screening and diagnosis
Prenatal Screening

• Advantages: anticipatory guidance, decisions about labour and delivery, further diagnostic investigations, interventions in-utero, termination of pregnancy (before 24 weeks)
  • Disadvantages: increased anxiety, knowledge is not necessarily power, inability to enjoy pregnancy, uncertain results, limitations of screening

blocks.html: Chromosome Disorders

• Turner Syndrome – puffy hands and feet at birth, webbed neck, coarctation of aorta, short stature, primary amenorrhea and infertility, normal intelligence; (45, X; 45, X/46, XX; 46, X, iXq; 45, X/46, XY)
  • Trisomy 13: Patau Syndrome – midline defects, cleft palate, polydactyly, severe developmental delay; (47, XX, +13)
  • Trisomy 18: Edward Syndrome – cardiac defects, delicate facial features, small size, overlapping fingers, “rocker bottom” feet, marked developmental delay; (47, XX, +18)
  • Klinefelter Syndrome – tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, learning disability, infertility, normal appearance; (47, XXY)
  • DiGeorge Syndrome – cleft palate, congenital heart defect, hypocalcemia, immunodeficiency; (22q11.2 microdeletion)
  • Prader-Willi Syndrome – hypotonia, hypogonadism, hypomentia, obesity (15q11-q13 paternal deletion)
  • Angelman Syndrome – small head, seizures, happy demeanor, stiff-legged gait with arms up, absent speech, severe developmental delay; (15q11-q13 maternal deletion)
Cytogenetic Tests

• Karyotype (G-banding): chromosomes of an individual arranged by pairs according to standard classification
  • Nomenclature: total number of chromosomes, sex chromosomes
  • Group A (1-3), Group B (4-5), Group C (6-12, X), Group D (acrocentric chromosomes: 13-15, 21, 22), Group E (16-18), Group F (19-20) Shows chromosome structure of genomic imbalance and balanced rearrangements
  • Order for suspected chromosome syndromes, first degree relatives with translocations, 3+ miscarriages, stillbirths or
  • neonatal death of unknown cause, disorders of sexual differentiation, infertility/amenorrhea
  • Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH): uses fluorescent probes that bind only to parts of the chromosome with a high degree of sequence complementarity
  • Microarray: measures the expression levels of large numbers of genes simultaneously Nomenclature: arr(1-22)x2, (XY)x1
  • ACMG: 1 = pathogenic, 2 = likely pathogenic, 3 = variant of uncertain clinical significance, 4 = likely benign, 5 = benign
  • Shows gene content of chromosome imbalance Order for moderate to severe developmental delays and multiple congenital anomalies
  • Quantitative fluorescence polymerase chain reaction (QF-PCR): amplifies specific regions of DNA and quantifies the amount of DNA present in those regions
Nutrients

• Macronutrients: carbon-based compounds that can be metabolically processed into cellular energy Carbohydrates (4Kcal/gram), protein (4Kcal/gram), lipids (9Kcal/gram) – alcohol (7Kcal/gram)
  • Micronutrients: not sources of energy for the body, but play a role as cofactors or coenzymes that facilitate chemical reactions Trace minerals: only required in a few mgs or less – molybdenum, selenium, zinc, iron, iodine
  • Macrominerals: required in hundreds of mgs – calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, phosphorus

blocks.html: Dietary Reference Intakes

• Estimated Average Requirement (EAR): meets the needs of 50% of the population
  • Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA): RDA = EAR + 2 SD; meets the needs of 97.5% of the population
  • Adequate Intake (AI): used when RDA cannot be calculated
  • Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL): highest level of daily nutrient intake that is unlikely to pose risk of adverse health effects to almost all individuals in the population
Canada’s Food Guide – Healthy Food Choices

• Eat plenty of vegetables and fruits, whole grain foods, and protein foods; choose proteins that come from plants more often Choose foods with healthy fats instead of saturated fat
  • Limit highly processed foods; if you choose these foods, eat them less often and in small amounts Prepare meals and snacks using ingredients that have little to no added sodium, sugars, or saturated fat
  • Choose healthier menu options when eating out
  • Make water your drink of choice
  • Replace sugary drinks with water
  • Use food labels
  • Be aware that food marketing can influence your choices
Canada’s Food Guide – Canada’s Dietary Guidelines

• 1. Nutritious foods are the foundation for healthy eating
  • 2. Processed or prepared foods and beverages that contribute to excess sodium, free sugars, or saturated fat undermine healthy eating and should not be consumed regularly
  • 3. Food skills are needed to navigate the complex food environment and support healthy eating
Dietary Trends

• Intermittent fasting – cycles between periods of fasting (alternate-day, whole-day, and/or time-restricted feeding), with either no food or significant calorie reduction, and periods of unrestricted eating
  • Gluten-free – eliminates all foods containing or contaminated with gluten
  • Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH diet) – fruits, vegetables, low fat milk, whole grains, fish, poultry, beans, nuts
  • Ketogenic diet – low-carbohydrate, high-fat
  • Mediterranean diet – primarily plant-based; emphasis on healthy fats; fish as the preferred animal protein; water as the main daily beverage; stresses daily physical activity
  • Paleo diet – caveman/Stone-Age diet, includes lean meats, fish, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds

blocks.html: Infant Nutrition

• Breastfeeding (exclusive up to 6 months, up to 2 years) + 400 IU/day Vitamin D + iron-containing foods after 6 months 20Kcal/oz, 0.67Kcal/mL – 50% fat, 40% lactose, 10% protein (60-80% whey protein, 20-40% casein)
  • Every 2-3 hours for 10-20 mins/side – high-fat hind milk important
  • Colostrum (IgA, IgM, IgG), transitional milk, mature milk
  • Iron supplementation for high-risk groups: birth weight < 3kg, premature infants < 37 weeks gestation, prenatal alcohol exposure, maternal diabetes, infants of iron-deficient mothers
  • Formula feeding – very important to mix formula correctly to avoid failure to thrive, electrolyte imbalance and/or dehydration
  • Ready to feed, concentration, powder
  • 20Kcal/oz, 0.67Kcal/mL – 50% fat, higher vitamin and mineral content than human milk, iron absorbed less Special formulas: hydrolyzed whey (lower osmolality, improve gastric emptying), soy (vegetarians, lactase deficiency,

  • Less stools than breastfed babies
Canadian Feeding Guidelines for 6-24 Months

• Open cups support development of mature feeding skills from > 6 months
  • No honey < 12 months – infantile botulism
  • Bottles and sippy cups are discouraged > 12 months
  • Homo milk can be given, but cannot replace breastmilk or formula
  • Start lumpy
  • Iron-containing foods – iron-fortified infant cereals, meat, tofu, legumes, poultry, fish, whole eggs
  • No delay in starting allergenic foods – eggs, peanut products
  • Parents decide what foods are available and when; children decide whether to eat or not and how much to eat

• Newborn: 5-10% weight loss 1-3 DOL, regain birth weight by 10-14 DOL

• A general term for a wide range of responses from the immune system within a localized tissue; systemic = sepsis

  • Acute inflammation – tissue repair, healing, and clearance of local pathogens
  • Resolution – shifts in cytokines, M1 to M2 macrophages

blocks.html: Antibody Function

• Neutralize – block the biological activity of the antigen by binding to its surface
  • Opsonize – bind to the surface antigen of the pathogen to facilitate phagocytosis
  • Facilitate pathogen recognition and antigenic responses – bind to specialized immune cells
  • Activate the complement system – phagocytosis and attracting other immune cells towards the pathogen
Immunization

• Immunologic memory: the immune system’s ability to remember its experience with an infectious agent, leading to effective and rapid immune response upon subsequent exposure to the same or similar infectious agents
  • Passive immunity – transfer of immunoglobulins obtained from human or animal sources, placental transfer
  • Active immunity – body produces pathogen-specific antibodies after an antigen is introduced through vaccines
General Approach to Childhood Behaviours

• Take a detailed history including the ABCs (antecedent, behaviour, consequence)
  • Ax development – make use of assessment tools
  • PEx – consider underlying physical conditions
  • Management plan – typical behaviour = anticipatory guidance; atypical behaviour = further Ax and specific Tx
Common Childhood Clinical Presentations

• Hidden causes of discomfort in young children: headache, undiagnosed seizures, entropion, otitis media, sinusitis, dental caries, mouth ulcers, pharyngitis, medication for asthma, GERD, constipation, UTI, renal stones, arthralgia/arthritis, occult fracture, hair tourniquet, eczema/dermatitis, skin breakdown/ulcer
  • Colic (5-20%) – increased frequency/intensity of crying in young infants who do not have underlying illness Prolonged crying (> 3 hours/day), persistent (> 3 days/week for > 3 weeks), especially evenings, peaks at 6 weeks
  • Tx: careful evaluation of causes for discomfort, reassurance, support/respite
  • Night waking (25%) – sleep patterns are highly variable in infancy; cultural expectations have a significant influence
  • Tx: sleep hygiene, appropriate limit setting, eliminate bottle at 12 months, reassurance/nurturing
  • Headbanging (under 2 years) – typically when a toddler is attention seeking, avoiding a request, or self-soothing
  • Management: careful Hx and PEx, encourage “time-in”, redirection/distraction
  • Infant masturbation (most children) – may be mistaken for seizures/movement disorder; quickly learn to keep “private”
  • Management: careful evaluation, caregiver education, encourage “time-in”, redirection/distraction
  • Temper tantrums (18-36 months) – out of control behaviour (screaming, stomping, hitting, headbanging, falling down, frustration/distress)
  • Part of normal assertion of independence and “testing” behaviour, brief (< 5 mins), improves with age, breath-holding
  • Management: careful evaluation, parent behaviour management strategies, consider DDx (sensory impairments, communication disorders, seizures, abuse/neglect, family violence, inappropriate expectations, neurological conditions, emerging mental health disorders)
  • Aggression/anger – requires a multimodal approach

blocks.html: School-Age Development (6-12 years)

• In pre-school years, there is semi-logical thinking which leads to misconceptions – “my parents divorced because I was bad”
  • School-age children start to differentiate from their parents; peers important, rule-based games, increased attention span
  • Learning disabilities, behaviour disorders, and intellectual disability may become evident during the school year
  • Increasing difficulty may occur as the educational demands increase
  • Mild deficits in learning may not present until school age
  • Diagnosing specific learning disabilities requires that the child have “significant” academic deficit – 2 grades below expectations
Factors Affecting School Readiness

• Physical health and fitness – hearing, vision, chronic conditions (surgical repairs of congenital disorders, medications)
  • Attitude and motivation – understand school is important and will be hard, able to delay gratification to some degree
  • Attentional readiness – sit and attend, know when to interrupt, listen without eye contact, assimilate verbal information
  • Emotional readiness – tolerate separation from parent, allow correction, make friends
  • Cognitive readiness – achievement of previous milestones
  • Cultural readiness – family feels school is important, school and family are congruent
  • Academic readiness – reading (rhyming), writing (fine motor dexterity), arithmetic (symbolic thinking, number concepts)
  • If a child is not going to be ready, try learning in smaller groups (preschool), remediation of identified deficits, delaying school entry, and/or specialized programming

blocks.html: Ideal Vaccines

• Safe with minimal adverse effects
  • Effective in providing lifelong protection against disease after a single dose that can be administered at birth
  • Inexpensive
  • Stable during shipment and storage
  • Easy to administer
Vaccines

• Individual level – protect the immunized person against the specific disease
  • Population level – reduce the incidence of disease; reduce exposure of susceptible individuals and consequent illness
  • Vaccine efficacy: the vaccine’s ability to prevent illness in people vaccinated in controlled studied
  • Vaccine effectiveness: the vaccine’s ability to prevent illness in people in the real world
Herd Immunity

• Herd immunity: the immunity of a population against a specific infectious disease
  • The resistance of a population to spread an infectious disease is based on the percentage of people who are immune and the probability that those who are still susceptible will come into contact with an infected person
  • The proportion of the population required to be immune to reach herd immunity depends on the transmissibility of the infectious agent either from a symptomatically infected person or from an asymptomatically colonized person
  • High R0 = diseases that are highly infectious and require higher immunization coverage – measles
